text: Picture a refinery on the Texas Gulf Coast at three in the morning. A flange on a high-pressure steam line has started to leak. It's hissing, it's getting worse, and the unit it feeds is making a lot of money every hour it runs.

speaker: JAMES
text: The plant manager has two options. Shut the unit down, cool everything, make the repair, then restart. That can take days and cost a fortune in lost production. Or call someone who can fix the leak while the line is still live, still hot, still under pressure.

speaker: NORA
text: That second option is what today's company does. Welcome to Portfolio Deep Dives, the show where we take one company at a time and look at its business, its market, its challenges and where AI could take it next. I'm Nora.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I'm James. Our series follows the companies in the portfolio of Levine Leichtman Capital Partners, a private equity firm based in Beverly Hills. Today it's the Colt Group, based in Pasadena, Texas, which has been doing on-line leak repair, hot tapping and related specialty services since 1981. And it's the newest company we'll cover in this series. The deal closed at the end of August 2026.

speaker: NORA
text: The usual note before we begin. speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk about the customer problem. Why is it so valuable to fix things without shutting down?
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: JAMES
text: Because in process industries, downtime is brutally expensive. A refinery unit, a chemical plant, a power station, a big pipeline, they're designed to run continuously. Shutting down isn't like turning off a light. You have to bring temperatures and pressures down safely, drain or purge lines, make the repair, then restart, which itself carries risk. Every hour offline is lost production.
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: NORA
text: So plants plan their shutdowns.
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: JAMES
text: They do. In the industry, a planned shutdown for major maintenance is usually called a turnaround. Plants schedule them carefully, sometimes years in advance, and pack a lot of work into them. The problem is what happens between turnarounds. Things leak. Valves fail. A new connection is needed for a project. If you can't wait for the next turnaround, you need a way to do the work live.
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: NORA
text: And that's where Colt comes in.
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the niche. Emergency and unplanned work where the asset has to stay in service. And because it's often urgent and high-stakes, the buyer is paying for speed and competence more than for the lowest price. That's our inference from the service model, but Colt's own site makes the same point by stressing certified procedures and expert technicians.
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: NORA
text: What about safety? Working on a live, pressurised line sounds dangerous.
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: JAMES
text: It is, and that's exactly why customers hire specialists. A leaking line of steam, hydrocarbons or chemicals is dangerous in itself. Doing anything to it while it's live requires engineered procedures, qualified people and strict controls. A good contractor reduces risk. A bad one can make a bad situation catastrophic. Safety record is one of the first things a plant will check before letting a contractor on site.
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: NORA
text: And these repairs, are they permanent?
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: JAMES
text: Often they're intended to be temporary, to keep the plant running safely until the next planned shutdown, when the component can be properly repaired or replaced. That's general industry practice. Which creates an interesting information problem. A big plant may have many temporary repairs in place at once, and someone has to keep track of where they are, how old they are and when they need permanent attention.
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: NORA
text: Which is exactly the kind of list a contractor could keep.
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly, and we'll come back to it, because it's a natural bridge from emergency work to an ongoing service.
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: NORA
text: And the water and utility side?
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: JAMES
text: Similar logic, different stakes. If a city needs to add a connection to a large water main, or isolate a section to repair it, shutting the main means cutting off customers. Hot tapping and line stopping let the utility keep water flowing while the work happens. The Garrison acquisition, a utility contractor, suggests Colt sees that as a growth area.
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: NORA
text: Who's the actual buyer inside a refinery?
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: JAMES
text: Usually maintenance and reliability teams, sometimes operations, and procurement for the contracts. In general terms, large plants often have approved contractor lists and master service agreements, so being on the list before the emergency happens matters enormously. When the leak starts at three a.m., nobody is running a tender. They call the firm they already trust.
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: NORA
text: What does being on that list actually involve?
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: JAMES
text: In general terms, a lot. Safety prequalification, insurance, documented procedures, training records for every technician, qualified welding procedures, often drug and alcohol testing programmes, and an acceptable safety performance history. Then on each visit, site inductions and work permits before anyone touches anything. It's a heavy administrative load, and it's also a barrier to entry. A new competitor can't just show up at a refinery gate.
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: NORA
text: And power and nuclear?
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: JAMES
text: Those can be even stricter. Nuclear sites in particular have demanding quality assurance rules for any contractor working on them. Colt lists power and nuclear as a market, but we didn't find details of its nuclear work, so I won't speculate on how big it is. The general point is that each segment has its own qualification hurdles, and clearing them takes years.
chapter: The problem: you can't shut it down

speaker: NORA
text: Let's go deeper on the services. Start with on-line leak repair.

speaker: JAMES
text: In general terms, the classic approach is to engineer an enclosure or clamp that fits around the leaking component, a flange, a valve, a section of pipe, and then inject a sealant compound into the enclosure under pressure to stop the leak. The trick is that every leak is a bit different. Different sizes, temperatures, pressures, fluids. So the enclosure usually has to be designed and made for that specific job, often very quickly.

speaker: NORA
text: Which is why the in-house engineering and fabrication matter.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. If you can take measurements on site, have an engineer design the clamp, and have your own shop machine it overnight, you can be back on site the next day. If you have to outsource that, you lose time.

speaker: NORA
text: Hot tapping?

speaker: JAMES
text: Hot tapping is making a new connection to a pipe while it's in service. You weld or bolt a fitting onto the outside of the live pipe, attach a valve and a special drilling machine, cut through the pipe wall inside a sealed chamber, then withdraw the cutter and close the valve. Now you have a new branch connection, and the main line never stopped.

speaker: NORA
text: And line stopping?

speaker: JAMES
text: Line stopping usually builds on a hot tap. Once you've got access into the pipe, you insert a plugging head that blocks the flow, so you can isolate a section downstream for repair or replacement, often with a temporary bypass to keep the product moving. When the work's done, you remove the plug and cap the fitting.

speaker: NORA
text: And field machining?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's taking machine tools to the equipment rather than taking the equipment to a machine shop. Resurfacing a damaged flange face in place, cutting and bevelling pipe, that kind of work. We'll actually cover a company that specialises in that in our next episode.

speaker: NORA
text: So what's common across all of these?

speaker: JAMES
text: Three things. Every job is a bit custom. Every job needs a qualified procedure and qualified people. And every job generates information. Measurements, drawings, materials, sealant choices, what worked, what didn't. Over forty-five years, that's a lot of information. Whether it's been captured well is the big question.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do the walk-through. A hypothetical call-out, invented customer, invented people.
chapter: A leak at three in the morning

speaker: JAMES
text: Let's go back to that refinery. The reliability engineer, call him Ray, sees a steam leak at a flange on a line feeding a processing unit. It's not catastrophic yet, but it's growing. He calls the leak repair contractor on his approved list, a company like Colt.
chapter: A leak at three in the morning

speaker: NORA
text: What happens next today?
chapter: A leak at three in the morning

speaker: JAMES
text: A dispatcher takes the call and asks the basics. What's leaking, the line size, the temperature, the pressure, the fluid. Then a technician drives out to the site, goes through the plant's safety induction and permits, and measures the flange carefully. Those measurements and photos go back to an engineer, who designs an enclosure and specifies a sealant suited to that temperature and fluid. The design goes to the shop, which machines the clamp, perhaps overnight.
chapter: A leak at three in the morning

speaker: NORA
text: And Ray's unit keeps running while that happens.
chapter: A leak at three in the morning

speaker: JAMES
text: It does, though the leak is being watched closely. Next day, the crew installs the enclosure and injects the sealant. The leak stops. The crew documents the job, the plant signs off, and an invoice follows. Ray adds a note to his maintenance system that this flange has a temporary repair to be addressed at the next turnaround.
chapter: A leak at three in the morning

speaker: NORA
text: Where's the time going?
chapter: A leak at three in the morning

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, three places. First, the information gathering. Back-and-forth between dispatcher, technician and engineer, getting the right details. Second, the engineering. Each design takes an engineer's time, even when the job is similar to one done before. Third, the paperwork after the job. Reports, records, invoicing.
chapter: A leak at three in the morning

speaker: NORA
text: Now replay it with AI.
chapter: A leak at three in the morning

speaker: JAMES
text: Ray calls in, and the dispatcher's system captures the details in a structured way, maybe even from a photo Ray sends. The system immediately searches Colt's records. Have we repaired this kind of flange, at this kind of temperature and pressure, with this fluid, before? Maybe even at this same refinery. It pulls up the five most similar past jobs: the clamp designs used, the sealants, any problems encountered.
chapter: A leak at three in the morning

speaker: NORA
text: So the engineer isn't starting from a blank page.
chapter: A leak at three in the morning

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. The engineer reviews the closest previous design, adapts it to the new measurements, and checks it. That could cut design time significantly, though we have no numbers to say how much. The technician arrives on site already knowing what's been tried at this facility. After the job, the system drafts the report from the technician's notes and photos, and the job record goes back into the knowledge base, better structured than before.
chapter: A leak at three in the morning

speaker: NORA
text: And the engineer still signs off.
chapter: A leak at three in the morning

speaker: JAMES
text: Always. This is safety-critical engineering on live, pressurised systems. The AI is a librarian and a drafting assistant. The professional engineer owns the design.
chapter: A leak at three in the morning

speaker: NORA
text: What does Ray, the customer, notice about the difference?
chapter: A leak at three in the morning

speaker: JAMES
text: Speed and confidence, mostly. The quote arrives faster and is grounded in similar past jobs. The crew turns up with a clamp that fits first time. And afterwards, Ray gets a clean digital record that slots into his own maintenance system, with the location, the design and a recommended date for permanent repair. When his next turnaround is being planned, that record is there, not lost in an email inbox.
chapter: A leak at three in the morning

speaker: NORA
text: So the benefit to Colt shows up as loyalty.
chapter: A leak at three in the morning

speaker: JAMES
text: Loyalty and share of wallet, in my view. The contractor whose records make the reliability engineer's job easier is the one who gets the next call, and probably a bigger slice of the turnaround work too. That's a hypothesis, but it's how relationships work in this kind of trade.

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find a reliable market size for on-line leak repair and hot tapping, so I won't give one. What we can say is that it's described by the new owner as fragmented, which means lots of smaller regional players. That's the precondition for a buy-and-build strategy.

text: What drives demand?

speaker: JAMES
text: Our inference is three things. Ageing industrial and pipeline infrastructure, which leaks and fails more as it gets older. Turnaround and shutdown schedules, because work that can't wait for the next turnaround needs an on-line solution. And safety and regulatory pressure to avoid both leaks and unplanned shutdowns. On the other side, demand is exposed to the investment cycles of oil and gas and petrochemicals.

text: This is general industry knowledge, since we couldn't verify competitors in our research. Team Incorporated is a listed industrial services company that offers leak repair and on-line services. text: What's the edge against a bigger competitor?

speaker: JAMES
text: Responsiveness and focus, in my view. In emergency work, the ability to get the right people and hardware to the site fast matters more than global scale. A firm that's close by, knows the plant, and can design and machine a clamp overnight wins the call. That's also why the integration of acquisitions matters so much. If Colt grows but gets slower, it loses its edge.

speaker: NORA
text: And are there AI-native challengers?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find any in leak repair itself. But there's a broader trend toward predictive maintenance, using sensors and historical data to anticipate failures. Monitoring and sensor startups could try to take the monitoring slice of the value chain, the part where you know a leak is coming before it starts. That's our inference, but it's directly relevant to ColtCONNECT.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's go segment by segment. How do the markets differ?

speaker: JAMES
text: Colt lists five broad areas. Refining and chemical is the core, in my view, given where Colt is based. That's high-temperature, high-pressure, often hazardous fluids, and plants that run around the clock. Downtime is very expensive, so the value of on-line repair is highest there.

speaker: NORA
text: Water?

speaker: JAMES
text: Municipal and industrial water is lower temperature and pressure, but the pipes are large and the customers can't be cut off. Hot tapping and line stopping are especially relevant, for new connections and isolating sections for repair. The buyer is often a public utility, which brings different procurement rules, more formal tenders, and slower decisions. Garrison, as a utility contractor, likely brings experience there.

speaker: NORA
text: And pipelines and utilities?

speaker: JAMES
text: Pipelines need hot taps and line stops when operators add connections or repair sections without stopping flow. Utilities, including gas distribution, need similar work on their networks. Power covers generating stations, where steam systems and cooling water lines leak just like they do in refineries. And through RJ Stacey, there's steel, with blast furnace repair. The mix matters because the segments move on different cycles. When refining slows, water and utilities may hold up, and the reverse.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk about the buy-and-build. What does the new owner actually do with a company like this?

speaker: JAMES
text: The stated plan is add-on acquisitions and investment in people, capabilities and geographic footprint. In practice, that typically means buying regional leak repair and hot tapping firms in areas where Colt is thin, adding capabilities like specialised machining or composites, and investing in the national network of crews and equipment.

speaker: NORA
text: What's the integration challenge?

speaker: JAMES
text: Every acquired firm has its own way of quoting, dispatching, documenting jobs and invoicing. Its own rate cards. Its own safety procedures, which need to be brought up to a common standard. Its own records of past jobs, probably in different formats, some on paper. RJ Stacey in Michigan and Garrison in New Jersey will each have their own systems and habits. And a company that has changed hands twice in a couple of years may have standardisation work still unfinished. That's our inference.

speaker: NORA
text: And why does that matter for AI?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because the knowledge base idea only works if records from every part of the group end up in one searchable, consistent place. If RJ Stacey's forty years of blast furnace repairs sit in a filing cabinet in Michigan, they don't help a technician in Texas. The integration project and the AI project are, in my view, the same project.

speaker: NORA
text: What about pricing?

speaker: JAMES
text: There's a straightforward opportunity to standardise rate cards across acquired businesses. When you buy small firms, you often find inconsistent pricing for similar work. Bringing that into line, carefully, is a classic buy-and-build lever. And over time, better data on job costs lets you price more accurately, which matters a lot in emergency work where quotes are often made fast.

speaker: NORA
text: Is quoting itself an AI opportunity?

speaker: JAMES
text: I think so. In emergency work, quotes are often made under time pressure, sometimes by phone, and the risk of underpricing a complex job is real. With good job-cost history, an assistant could suggest a price range based on similar past jobs: size, temperature, pressure, fluid, travel distance, likely crew size, fabrication needed. The estimator still decides, but starts from evidence rather than instinct. Over hundreds of jobs a year, more accurate quoting adds up.

text: Break down the data a bit more. What kinds of data does a company like Colt have?

text: In my view, three kinds. First, job history. Every call-out, with the site, the equipment, the conditions, the design, the materials, the outcome. That's the knowledge base raw material. Second, monitoring data, if ColtCONNECT collects it, which is time-series sensor readings from customer equipment. That's the predictive raw material. text: Linking them. A great job history is far more useful if it's linked to the monitoring data from the same flange and the cost of each repair. That linking only happens if someone designs it. Most field services firms collect all three types of data in separate systems that never talk to each other. That's our inference about the industry generally, not a finding about Colt.
chapter: Where Colt is with AI and data

speaker: NORA
text: Let's name the challenges. What's hard for Colt, in your view?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd name five. First, key-person dependence. Specialty services businesses depend heavily on experienced technicians and engineers, and a founder-era company may also depend heavily on a few senior leaders. If knowledge isn't captured, retirements and departures hurt.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Integration. A buy-and-build adds firms with different systems, prices and cultures. Doing that fast without diluting the responsiveness Colt sells is genuinely hard.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Cyclicality. Refining, chemicals and pipelines go through investment cycles. When oil prices fall or margins tighten, plants cut maintenance spending where they can. Emergency repairs can't be cut, but planned work and projects can be deferred. Diversification into water, utilities, power and steel helps, but the core is still energy and process industry.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth.

speaker: JAMES
text: Workforce. Certified welders and skilled field technicians are in demand across many industries, and the work involves travel, odd hours and hazardous conditions. Recruiting and keeping them is a constant challenge, though we didn't find Colt-specific data on it.

speaker: NORA
text: And how long does it take to make a good leak repair technician?

speaker: JAMES
text: We don't have a figure for Colt, but in general, skilled trades like this take years to master. You learn by doing jobs alongside experienced people, seeing many kinds of leaks, learning what works on which fluid at which temperature. That apprenticeship model is slow, and it depends on the senior people having time to teach. In my view, this is one of the most underrated places for AI. Not replacing the apprenticeship, but giving a newer technician access to the experience of the whole company when the senior person isn't standing next to them.

speaker: NORA
text: And fifth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Turning emergency work into recurring revenue. Emergency call-outs are valuable but lumpy and hard to forecast. Investors generally value recurring, contracted revenue more highly. The challenge, and the opportunity, is to build more predictable revenue streams, which is where monitoring comes in.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there an AI-specific challenge?

speaker: JAMES
text: Data quality and trust. Technicians and engineers in safety-critical work are rightly sceptical of tools that might be wrong. A knowledge base that surfaces an inappropriate past repair as a template could mislead someone. So the tools need to be designed as aids to qualified people, with clear provenance, and introduced with the engineers rather than imposed on them.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk opportunities. Where would you look first?

speaker: JAMES
text: The first is AI-assisted repair engineering, the knowledge base we walked through. Every past job, procedure, design and engineer's note, searchable by the characteristics of the leak. The value lever is labour hours, faster estimates and less rework, and faster response, which is what customers pay for.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: A predictive offering built on ColtCONNECT. If Colt can install monitoring on customers' at-risk equipment, flanges with past repairs, ageing lines, critical valves, and alert them before a leak becomes an emergency, that turns ad hoc call-outs into a contracted service. The value lever is recurring revenue and margin. And it changes the relationship from the firm you call when things go wrong to the firm that helps you keep things from going wrong.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's make that one concrete too. A second walk-through.

speaker: JAMES
text: Sure. Invented example again. A chemical plant has a history of leaks on a few dozen flanges in a hot service area, many of which have temporary repairs waiting for the next turnaround. Today, the plant waits for leaks to appear, then calls for help. With a monitoring subscription, sensors are installed on the highest-risk points, measuring things like temperature or acoustic signals that can indicate a developing leak.

speaker: NORA
text: And then?

speaker: JAMES
text: A dashboard shows the plant, and Colt, which points are stable and which are trending. When one starts to drift, Colt's team gets an alert, checks the history of that flange in its records, and calls the plant to suggest an inspection or a planned repair before it becomes a three a.m. emergency. Colt might even pre-fabricate the enclosure because the dimensions are already on file.

speaker: NORA
text: So the plant pays a monthly fee for fewer emergencies.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the idea. And it also feeds the turnaround plan. Before the next shutdown, Colt can give the plant a prioritised list of every temporarily repaired point and its condition. In my view, that's a much more valuable relationship than waiting for the phone to ring. But I want to be clear, this is a hypothesis. We don't know how far ColtCONNECT already goes toward it.

speaker: NORA
text: What about the risk of cannibalising emergency revenue?

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a real tension. If monitoring prevents emergencies, Colt does fewer high-margin emergency jobs. But in my view, someone will sell plants predictive monitoring anyway. Better for Colt to own that relationship than to lose it to a sensor startup. And planned repairs are still repairs, just scheduled, and probably more efficient to deliver.

speaker: NORA
text: Third opportunity?

speaker: JAMES
text: Dispatch and scheduling optimisation across a national network. Which crew, with which equipment and qualifications, can reach which site fastest? As Colt grows through acquisitions, that becomes a harder problem and a bigger lever. The key measure is emergency response time, along with labour and travel cost.

speaker: NORA
text: What else?

speaker: JAMES
text: The stated ones: more add-on acquisitions in uncovered regions, and investment in geographic footprint. Standardised rate cards across acquired businesses. And cross-selling Colt's manufacturing and fabrication capacity, the CNC and composites work, to existing repair customers. Plus, in my view, a fairly simple one: AI-drafted job reports and invoices from technicians' notes and photos, which saves time and speeds up cash collection.

speaker: NORA
text: You hinted at training earlier.

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. The same knowledge base that helps an engineer design a clamp can help train a new technician. Short case studies drawn from real past jobs: here's the leak, here's what we did, here's what went wrong the first time and why. Built into onboarding, that could shorten the time to competence. It's also a recruiting message. Join us and you'll learn from forty-five years of jobs, not just from whoever happens to be on your crew.

speaker: NORA
text: This is the episode where the hundred-day question is literal. The deal just closed. What should the first hundred days look like?
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd split it into three tracks: understand, quick wins, and set up the big bet. Days one to thirty are mostly understanding. Meet the field leaders, engineers and the leaders of the acquired businesses. Map how a job flows today in each business, from the call to the invoice. Inventory the data: where are the historical job records, in what format, how complete. And find out exactly what ColtCONNECT is, where it's installed and what it measures.
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: NORA
text: And quick wins?
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: JAMES
text: Days thirty to sixty. Pick one or two things that make technicians' and engineers' lives easier fast, because that builds trust. For example, a common digital job report format across the group, with AI drafting from notes and photos. Or a simple searchable archive of past repair designs from the main engineering office. Something people can use within weeks.
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: NORA
text: And setting up the big bet?
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: JAMES
text: Days sixty to a hundred. Decide, based on what you learned, which of the two big bets to fund first: the repair knowledge base or the predictive monitoring service. Pick an owner. Agree how you'll measure it. And pick pilot customers or a pilot region.
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: NORA
text: So which bet would you pick?
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: JAMES
text: If the historical records are reasonably complete and digital, the repair knowledge base first. It uses data Colt already owns, it helps the people who are the core of the business, it improves response speed immediately, and it doesn't need customers to buy anything new. Value lever: engineering and technician hours, faster quotes, fewer repeat call-outs.
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: NORA
text: And if the records are a mess?
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: JAMES
text: Then step one is digitising and structuring the records, which is itself useful, and starting predictive monitoring with a few willing customers in parallel. Monitoring generates new, clean data from day one. Either way, both bets reinforce each other. The knowledge base tells you what failed and how it was fixed. Monitoring tells you what's about to fail.
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: NORA
text: How would you run the knowledge base pilot?
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: JAMES
text: Start with the Gulf Coast engineering team. Load the last several years of job records, designs and photos. Have engineers use the search on every new job for a couple of months and log, for each job, whether it found something useful and how much time it saved. Have senior engineers review the results. If engineers say it's saving them real time, extend it to the acquired businesses and make adding records a standard part of closing every job.
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: NORA
text: Who owns it?
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: JAMES
text: A senior engineer with credibility in the field, paired with someone who can handle the data and tools. If it's seen as a head-office IT project, technicians will ignore it. If it's seen as the engineering team's own tool, they'll feed it.
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: NORA
text: And governance?
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: JAMES
text: From day one: every design is still reviewed and approved by a qualified engineer, the tool shows the source of every suggestion, and customer data from one plant is handled under that customer's terms. Many refineries and pipelines are critical infrastructure with strict rules on data and site information. A clear policy written early is much easier than one written after a problem.
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: NORA
text: And what about the technicians themselves? These are people working on pipe racks, not at desks.
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a crucial design point. Any tool for the field has to work on a phone or a rugged tablet, often with gloves on, in noise, heat and sometimes poor signal. Voice notes and photos are far more practical than typing. An assistant that turns a technician's thirty-second voice note and four photos into a structured job record would be used. A long form would not.
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: NORA
text: So the interface matters as much as the intelligence.
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: JAMES
text: In field services, it often matters more. The best model in the world is useless if the technician won't open it at the end of a twelve-hour shift. Design for the worst moment of the worst day, and you'll get adoption.
chapter: The first 100 days and the best AI bet

speaker: NORA
text: Let's step back. What can other businesses learn from Colt?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four lessons. First, your job history is a hidden asset. Every field services company has years of records about what broke and how it was fixed. Most treat them as paperwork. Structured and searchable, they become a competitive advantage that a new entrant can't buy.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, the first hundred days set the data foundations. When a new owner arrives, it's the best moment to agree a common way of recording jobs across every business, because everyone expects change. Wait two years, and every acquired business has dug in on its own habits.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, move from reactive to predictive where you can. Emergency work is valuable, but recurring, contracted service is more valuable and more predictable. If your customers would pay to avoid the emergency, find a way to sell them that.

speaker: NORA
text: And fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, build AI with the experts, not for them. In safety-critical work, engineers and technicians are the people whose trust you need. Give them tools that make them faster and better, show them where every suggestion came from, and let them own the review. Then they'll make the tools better.

speaker: NORA
text: I'd add one. Don't let growth slow you down.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a good one. A business that sells speed has to make sure each acquisition makes it faster, not slower. Dispatch, shared engineering and a shared knowledge base are how you make scale an advantage rather than a burden.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk risks.

speaker: JAMES
text: One, AI-enabled entrants. Sensor and monitoring startups could take the predictive slice of the value chain, leaving Colt with only the emergency work. Two, customer insourcing. If AI-guided procedures make some routine repairs easier, larger plants might do more themselves, reducing call volumes. Both of those are our inferences, not things we've seen happen.

speaker: NORA
text: Three?

speaker: JAMES
text: Three, integration risk. Rapid add-ons can dilute the responsiveness and safety standards that Colt sells. One serious safety incident at an acquired business would hurt the whole brand. Four, cyclicality in oil, gas and petrochemical spending. And five, execution risk on technology. Building a knowledge base or a monitoring service takes investment and focus, in a company whose core skill is field work, not software.

speaker: NORA
text: And cybersecurity? If Colt starts connecting sensors on customers' plants, that's a new exposure.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a serious one. Refineries, pipelines, power plants and water systems are critical infrastructure, and their operators are very careful about anything connecting to their networks. A monitoring service has to be designed with security from the start, probably with sensors on separate networks from the plant's control systems, strong access controls, and a clear agreement on who owns the data. Get that wrong, and you don't just lose a contract, you damage the trust that the whole business rests on. Get it right, and a strong security story becomes part of the sales pitch.

speaker: NORA
text: And for the owners?

speaker: JAMES
text: It's the beginning of the hold, so the risk is mostly about setting the right course. Buying a platform in a fragmented market pays off if the add-ons and the operating improvements come through. The upside case, in my view, is a national specialist with a shared knowledge base, faster response and a growing recurring monitoring business. That's a different and more valuable company than a collection of regional repair shops.

speaker: NORA
text: What should listeners watch?

speaker: JAMES
text: Three things. First, the first add-on under the new owner, and where it is. That tells you the geographic priority. Second, any announcement about ColtCONNECT, new customers, new capabilities, or a subscription offering. And third, any sign of investment in digital systems, a common job platform or a technology leadership hire. Any of those would show the AI story moving from possible to real.

speaker: NORA
text: Quick-fire round. Short answers.

speaker: JAMES
text: Go.

speaker: NORA
text: What does Colt sell?

speaker: JAMES
text: Keeping the plant running while the pipe gets fixed.

speaker: NORA
text: Most valuable asset?

speaker: JAMES
text: Forty-five years of repair know-how, plus in-house engineering and fabrication.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest weakness?

speaker: JAMES
text: Very little public data, and probably a lot of knowledge living in people's heads.

speaker: NORA
text: Shipped AI feature?

speaker: JAMES
text: None we found. ColtCONNECT monitoring is the closest thing, and its depth isn't verified.

speaker: NORA
text: Best AI bet?

speaker: JAMES
text: A searchable repair knowledge base, then predictive monitoring as a subscription.

speaker: NORA
text: Will AI replace the leak repair technician?

speaker: JAMES
text: No. Nobody's sending a chatbot up a pipe rack. It will make the technician faster and better informed.

speaker: NORA
text: One thing a refinery reliability manager should ask their contractor this year?

speaker: JAMES
text: Can you show me every temporary repair you've done at my site and its condition?

speaker: NORA
text: Optimist or pessimist?

speaker: JAMES
text: Optimist. It's a needed service with real know-how, and the new owner has arrived at exactly the right moment to set up the data foundations.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me try a summary. The Colt Group, founded in 1981 and based in Pasadena, Texas, repairs leaks and modifies pipework on live industrial systems, through on-line leak repair, hot tapping, line stopping and field machining, for refineries, chemical plants, pipelines, power, utilities and water systems. Under Capstreet it added RJ Stacey in Michigan and Garrison Enterprise in New Jersey, and in late August 2026 Levine Leichtman bought it, with chief executive Jason Box staying on as a significant investor and a plan to grow through acquisitions and new geography. We found no explicit AI at Colt, but it claims historical digital records and offers a monitoring technology called ColtCONNECT. The best opportunities, in our view, are a searchable repair knowledge base and a predictive monitoring subscription. The challenges are integration, key-person dependence, cyclicality and turning emergency work into recurring revenue.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's it. And the lesson for anyone in field services is that the call you answered at three in the morning, every one of them for forty-five years, is data. Capture it well, and it becomes the reason customers call you first.

speaker: NORA
text: Next time on Portfolio Deep Dives, episode twenty, we stay in the field with In-Place Machining, a Milwaukee company that brings the machine shop to the machine.

speaker: JAMES
text: See you then.
